blocks.text: The previous topic introduced instruction as one of the four core parts of prompt anatomy, this topic goes deep on that one component specifically, what actually makes an instruction clear, specific, and effective at directing a model toward the task you genuinely want performed.

This topic covers specificity, strong task defining verbs, the difference between describing a situation and actually instructing an action, and where an instruction should sit within a larger prompt for maximum effect.
1. What Makes an Instruction an Instruction

blocks.alt: What Makes an Instruction an Instruction
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064317-867207596.png

An instruction is the part of a prompt that tells the model what task to perform, summarize, translate, classify, rewrite, extract, without a clear instruction, the model has to infer the task from context alone, which produces inconsistent results across different inputs.
2. Specificity Beats Vagueness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064318-689229646.png

"Help with this" leaves the model to guess what kind of help you actually want, "Fix the grammar errors in this paragraph without changing its meaning" removes that guesswork entirely, the more specifically an instruction names the exact action and its boundaries, the more consistently the model performs it.

code.content:
vague = "Help with this email."
specific = "Rewrite this email to sound more concise and professional, keeping the same key points."

blocks.text: 3. Choosing Strong, Task Defining Verbs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064318-900903408.png

Weak verbs like look at or think about leave the actual expected action ambiguous, strong, specific verbs, classify, extract, summarize, translate, rank, compare, directly name the operation you want performed, making the instruction far less open to interpretation.

blocks.text: 4. One Clear Instruction vs Several Bundled Ones

blocks.alt: One Clear Instruction vs Several Bundled Ones
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064319-912144154.png

Cramming several distinct tasks into one ambiguous sentence, "summarize and also check for errors and maybe suggest improvements", tends to produce a response that handles some of those tasks well and others poorly, breaking distinct instructions into clearly separated, explicit steps generally produces a more complete and reliable result.
5. Instructions vs Mere Descriptions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064576-19987588.png

Simply describing the situation, "this is a customer support ticket", is not the same as instructing an action, "classify this ticket priority as low, medium, or high", a prompt that only describes without actually instructing leaves the model without a clear task to perform.

blocks.title: This distinction trips up a lot of early prompt attempts
blocks.content: It is easy to write several sentences of accurate description and assume the model will infer what to do with it, an explicit instruction removes that assumption entirely.

blocks.text: 6. Where an Instruction Should Sit in a Prompt

blocks.alt: Where an Instruction Should Sit in a Prompt
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064578-330416884.png

Placing the instruction near the beginning of a prompt, before a large block of context or input, tends to produce more consistent results than burying it at the very end, this connects directly back to the generation mechanics covered in the earlier How LLMs Process Prompts topic, an early instruction shapes how the model interprets everything that follows it.
7. Testing Whether an Instruction Is Clear Enough

A practical test, read only the instruction sentence on its own, without any of the surrounding context or input, if it is not immediately obvious what specific action is being requested, the instruction likely needs to be more specific.
8. Common Instruction Failure Patterns

Instructions commonly fail by being too vague to pin down a specific action, by bundling multiple distinct tasks into one ambiguous sentence, or by describing a situation without ever actually issuing a directive, all three failure patterns share the same fix, state plainly and specifically what action the model should take.
9. Instruction as the Anchor for the Rest of the Prompt

blocks.alt: Instruction as the Anchor for the Rest of the Prompt
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064578-909736720.png

A clear instruction does more than just specify the task, it acts as an anchor the model uses to interpret every other part of the prompt, the context, the input, and the output format all get read through the lens of what the instruction says the actual goal is.
Worked Example
A developer writes "Look at this resume" as an instruction, hoping the model will extract key skills. The response comes back as a generic, unfocused summary of the entire resume.

Rewriting the instruction as "Extract the candidate top 5 technical skills as a bulleted list" produces exactly the focused output needed, the change from a weak, vague verb to a specific, strong one is the entire difference between the two results.
Common Mistakes

items: Using weak, vague verbs like look at or think about instead of specific action verbs like extract or classify
Bundling several distinct tasks into a single ambiguous sentence instead of clearly separated instructions
Writing extensive description of the situation without ever issuing an actual directive
Burying the instruction at the end of a long prompt instead of placing it near the beginning

blocks.text: Practice

Take an instruction you have written before that used a weak verb like help with or look at, rewrite it using a specific, strong action verb, and test whether the resulting output is more consistently aligned with what you actually wanted.
Key Takeaway

An effective instruction names a specific, single action using a strong verb, is placed early in the prompt, and actually directs a task rather than just describing a situation, making it the anchor the model uses to interpret every other part of the prompt correctly.
